blocks.text:
Sandra Little
Director of Operations
Salazar-Mendoza
Dear Ms. Little,

This letter sets out the terms on which Saltmarsh Environmental Partners will carry out the sediment sampling program we discussed for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, and it asks for your countersignature so that a signed copy can go into the file before any work begins. I have kept it plain on purpose. Where a clause below reads as boilerplate, it is there because it has earned its place over many engagements, and not because a form demanded it.

The program covers the collection and laboratory analysis of sediment at the stations we agreed during our site visit. Samples will be collected under chain of custody, delivered to an accredited laboratory, and analyzed for the parameters set out in our scope discussion. The field method is a settled one, and we will follow it as written rather than improvising on site, so that a reviewer reading the record years from now can see exactly what was done, where, and when.

Results will be compiled in a data workbook, with each result tied to its station, its sample identifier, and the date it was taken. I check the totals in that workbook against the laboratory reports myself before anything is issued, because a figure I have not verified is a figure I would not be able to defend, and the value of this kind of work rests on being able to defend it. The program closes with a summary letter report that states what was measured, where, and when, and stops there. We do not editorialize a finding, and where the data leave a question open we will say so plainly rather than paper over it.

You will work mainly with two of our people. John Sanchez, our Senior Scientist, leads the technical side of the program and is responsible for the sampling design, the laboratory coordination, and the report. Heather Morton, our Field Technician, runs the sampling rounds and keeps the field record, which on a program like this is as much a deliverable as the numbers themselves. I sign what leaves this office and review the workbook before submission, so my name will be on the final report alongside theirs.

You will not have to chase us for status. We will send a short written report at about the midpoint and again as we near the end, and there will be a working session or two along the way with your site contact, so that nothing about access or scheduling has to be settled by email at the last minute. If a result ever looks like it needs your attention before the final report, you will hear it from us when we see it, not at delivery.

At the close of the program you will have three things: the summary report, the data workbook that stands behind it, and the field record for every round. The report is the document you would hand to an agency; the workbook and the field record are what let anyone, including a reviewer years from now, check the report against what was actually done. We keep copies of all three, and all three are yours.

Because the estuary is tidal, the rounds are planned around the water and the weather rather than the calendar, so that each sample is clean and comparable with the last. That sometimes means a round moves by a day or two; when it does, Heather will let your site contact know in advance. None of that changes the fixed fee, and none of it changes the stations or the method, which stay the same from the first round to the last.

The fee for the program is a fixed {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}, which covers the field collection, the laboratory analysis at the agreed parameter list, the data workbook, and the summary report. It does not cover work outside that scope, and if something on the site turns out to call for more than we have described here, I will tell you before we do it rather than after. We are prepared to begin on {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}}, subject to site access and to conditions on the estuary.
Fees and Payment

The fixed fee is invoiced in two parts: half on commencement and the balance on delivery of the summary report. Invoices are due within thirty days. Laboratory analysis is included at the parameter list we agreed; analysis added at your request beyond that list is billed at cost, and only after you have approved the addition in writing.
Term and Termination

The engagement runs from commencement until the summary report is delivered and accepted. Either of us may end it on fifteen days' written notice. If you end it partway through, you owe us for the fieldwork completed and the laboratory work already committed to that point, and we will hand over the field record and any data in hand so that nothing done so far is lost.
Confidentiality

We treat the site data, your business information, and the fact of this engagement as confidential, and we do not discuss them outside the firm without your consent. The one exception is a disclosure required by law or by an agency with jurisdiction over the site, and in that event we will tell you what is being disclosed and to whom, so far as we are permitted to.
Limitation of Liability

Our work rests on the conditions found at the sampling stations on the days they were sampled, and sediment conditions can vary across a site and over time. Our liability for the engagement is limited to the amount of the fee, and we are not responsible for decisions others make on the basis of the report beyond what the data in it actually support. This is not a hedge against doing the work carefully; it is a plain recognition of what a sampling program can and cannot tell you.
Governing Law
This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which the site sits, and any dispute under it will be resolved there.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign below and return one copy to me, keeping the other for your file. If anything here reads differently from what we discussed, call me before you sign and we will settle it then. I am glad to be doing this work with you, and I think the record it produces will be one you can rely on.

To: Sediment sampling team
From: John Sanchez, Senior Scientist
Re: Salazar-Mendoza sediment program, getting started

Our aim on this one is simple to state and worth stating plainly: we are building a sediment dataset for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} that will hold up when someone reads it years from now, with every result tied to a station, a sample, and a date. Everything below serves that aim. If a step does not make the record cleaner or more defensible, we should question whether it belongs at all.

This is field-heavy work on a tidal estuary, which means the schedule bends to the water rather than the other way around. I would rather we plan the rounds around the tide from the start than fight the site halfway through. We have done enough of these to know where the friction usually is, and most of it is avoidable with a little order up front.

A word on why we are careful to the point of tedium here. The people who will lean on this dataset are not in the room with us; an agency reviewer, or the next consultant on the site, may open the workbook years out with no one left to ask what a note meant. So we write the record for that reader and not for ourselves, and we make it legible without us.
How the work divides

items: Sampling design and station layout, finalized against the site we walked, so that every round samples the same points in the same way.
Field collection and chain of custody. Heather Morton runs the rounds and keeps the field record, and that record is a deliverable as much as the numbers are.
Laboratory coordination: sample submission, turnaround, and reconciling what comes back against what we sent.
The data workbook, where results are entered, tied to their stations, and checked. Totals are verified before anything leaves the office.
The summary report, which states what was measured, where, and when, and does not reach past the data.

blocks.text: The order of that list matters less than the discipline behind it. A clean field record makes the workbook straightforward; a clean workbook makes the report nearly write itself. Most of the care belongs at the front end, in the field, where a mistake is cheap to fix and expensive to discover later.

A note on coordination, since it is where a small team either gains or loses its advantage. Field notes go into the workbook promptly, not at the end of the month; a question about a station or a sample comes to me while the round is still fresh in mind. The dataset is only ever as good as the least careful handoff in it, and on a program that lives this long in the file, the handoffs are worth getting right the first time.

We begin on {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}}. Before then, I want the station list and the sampling plan settled, the laboratory lined up for our first submission, and the field kit checked over. Heather and I will walk the round order this week so that the first day on site is spent sampling and not deciding.

Our point of contact at Salazar-Mendoza is Sandra Little, their Director of Operations. She handles site access and scheduling on their end, so if a round has to move for the tide or the weather, she is the one to tell, and to tell early. Let us keep her in the loop the way we would each want to be kept in the loop.

That is the whole of it for now. Bring me anything that looks off on site rather than quietly working around it; on a program like this, the small things caught early are exactly what keep the record clean. — John Sanchez
Working Session, Sediment Sampling Program

These are the minutes of a working session held to review progress on the sediment sampling program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}. This was the first review since the program began, and the purpose of the session was to confirm what the first sampling round produced, settle two open items on site access, and agree the next round. The notes follow the order the session took, and each item is recorded with its owner so that nothing agreed here is left without a name against it.
Present:

items: John Sanchez, Senior Scientist, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Heather Morton, Field Technician, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Sandra Little, Director of Operations, Salazar-Mendoza

blocks.text: First round completed. The first sampling round was completed at the agreed stations, under chain of custody, and the samples were delivered to the laboratory. One station was sampled a day later than planned because of the tide; the shift was logged, and it does not affect the comparability of the data.

Field record. Heather Morton confirmed that the field notebook and the station log are current through the first round, with sample times, station identifiers, and field conditions recorded for each point. The record is being kept in the standard format, so that this round and the next will read the same way side by side.

Laboratory turnaround. Results for the first round are expected back within the standard turnaround window. John Sanchez noted that once they arrive, each result will be entered against its station and sample identifier and reconciled against the submission record before anything is reported.

Site access. Access to the two upstream stations has been intermittent. Sandra Little agreed to arrange standing access for the field crew so that a round is not held up at the gate, and to give the crew a direct contact for the days they are on site.

Field conditions. The crew reported that footing at the two upstream stations is poor at low water, and that those points are safer and cleaner to sample on a rising tide. The round order will be set accordingly, which has the added benefit of keeping the samples comparable from one visit to the next.

Data workbook. The workbook has been set up with the full station list and the sample identifiers already in place, so that first-round results can be entered directly on receipt from the laboratory. Totals will be reconciled against the laboratory reports before any figure is shared outside the firm.

Next round. The group agreed to schedule the second round around the next suitable tide window rather than to a fixed date, on the same station list and the same method, so that the two rounds remain directly comparable.

rows: Enter and check first-round results on receipt from the laboratory
Arrange standing site access and a day-of contact for the crew
Confirm the tide window and schedule the second round
Keep the field record current for each round

blocks.text: The single next step is the second sampling round: once Sandra Little confirms access and the tide window is set, the crew will run it on the same stations and by the same method as the first.
Status Report, Sediment Sampling Program

The sediment sampling program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} is on schedule and roughly at its midpoint, and there is nothing on it that needs your attention beyond this note. The fieldwork is running as planned, the early results are in hand and checked, and we remain on track to deliver the summary report as scoped. What follows sets out where we are in a little more detail.
Accomplishments this period

Since the program began, the field crew has completed the early rounds on schedule, and the samples have moved through the laboratory without a break in the chain of custody. Heather Morton has kept the field record current round by round, so the station log, the sample times, and the field conditions are all in hand and legible, which is a large part of what makes the eventual report defensible. The data workbook has been built and populated with the results received so far, each tied to its station and sample and reconciled against the laboratory reports.
Where things stand

We have completed the early sampling rounds at the agreed stations, all under chain of custody, and those samples have been through the laboratory. Heather Morton has run each round at the Salazar-Mendoza stations on the same method, so the data collected so far is directly comparable, which is the property the whole program depends on. Results received to date have been entered against their stations and sample identifiers and reconciled against the laboratory reports.

One round shifted by a day for the tide, which is ordinary on this estuary and was logged so that the record stays clean. Nothing in the results so far is surprising or out of range for a site like yours. I would not read much into a half-finished dataset, though, and I am not going to characterize the findings until the program is complete and the numbers can be read together.

On the data itself, I will say only what it can carry at this stage. The results in hand are internally consistent and fall within the range we would expect for a site of this kind, and none of the early rounds turned up anything that would change the plan for the rest of the program. That is a statement about the shape of the data, not a finding, and I would ask you to read it as the former.
Budget

The program is a fixed-fee engagement of {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}, and our effort to date tracks the plan. We have committed roughly half of the fee, in line with being about halfway through the work, and I do not foresee anything in the remaining scope that would change the figure. If something on the site did call for work beyond what we scoped, you would hear it from me before it was done, and not on the final invoice.
What comes next

The remaining sampling rounds will be run on the same stations and by the same method as the completed ones, scheduled around the tide rather than to fixed dates so that each sample stays clean and comparable. As those results come back, they will be entered and checked the same way, and the data workbook will be built out toward the full set. The summary report is drafted last, once every round is in and the totals have been verified.

There is nothing in the remaining scope that we have not done many times before, and I mention that not to be reassuring but because it is true: the second half of a program like this is mostly a matter of holding to the method that produced the first half. The one thing I will watch is consistency across the full set, so that the last round reads against the first without an asterisk.
Risks, and how we are handling them

The main variable is the weather and the tide, which can move a round by a day or two. We manage it by planning the rounds around the water rather than fighting it, and by keeping enough margin in the schedule that a short delay does not put the delivery at risk. Laboratory turnaround is the other variable; it has stayed within the normal window so far, and we submit promptly after each round to keep it there.

None of these rises to a concern today. I mention them because a status report that lists no risks is usually one that has not looked, and I would rather name the ordinary ones plainly than leave you to wonder whether we had thought about them at all.

I will send the next report at about the three-quarter mark, or sooner if anything changes that you should know about before then. In the meantime, if a question occurs to you, the fastest answer is to call me directly. — John Sanchez, Senior Scientist
Minutes: Sediment Sampling Program, Closeout Review

These minutes record a working session held to walk through the closeout of the sediment sampling program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}. With the field program essentially complete, the session covered the final round, the state of the data workbook, and the steps left before the summary report is submitted. The notes follow the order of the discussion.
Present:

items: John Sanchez, Senior Scientist, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Heather Morton, Field Technician, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Sandra Little, Director of Operations, Salazar-Mendoza

blocks.text: Final round. The final sampling round has been completed at the agreed stations, under chain of custody, and the samples are now with the laboratory. Every round was run on the same stations and by the same method, so the full dataset is comparable end to end, and the field record is complete and current through the last visit.

Data workbook. Results received to date have been entered against their stations and sample identifiers. The remaining results, from the final round, will be entered on receipt, after which the workbook totals will be reconciled against the laboratory reports and checked. No figure leaves the office until those totals have been verified.

Reconciliation and review. The workbook totals will be reconciled against the laboratory reports and reviewed internally before the report is issued, which is the standard check on any number that goes to a client or an agency. This is the step that most often catches a transposed figure, and it is not skipped for a program running late or a program running early.

Summary report. John Sanchez reported that the summary report is in draft and will be completed once the final results are in and the workbook has been checked. It will state what was measured, where, and when, without reaching past the data, consistent with how the program was scoped at the outset.

Archived record. Heather Morton confirmed that the complete field record, covering every round from the first to the last, will be filed alongside the workbook and the report, so that the program can be reconstructed from the record alone if it is ever questioned. The record is current and needs no reworking before it is filed.

Submission logistics. Sandra Little confirmed how Salazar-Mendoza would like the final report delivered and who should receive it on their side. She asked for a short walkthrough at delivery, and John Sanchez agreed to provide one.

Remaining work. The group noted that the program is in its final stretch, with the fieldwork done and only the reconciliation, the report, and delivery still to come. No new work was identified during the session, and none of the remaining steps depends on further access to the site.

rows: Enter final-round results and reconcile the workbook totals
Confirm the field record is complete for all rounds
Finish the summary report after totals are verified

blocks.text: The single next step is reconciliation: once the final-round results return from the laboratory, the workbook totals are checked, and the summary report is finished and submitted to Salazar-Mendoza.
